items.title: Gene Bertoncini interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001
items.q: And Skitch Henderson was on piano. And Peter Appleyard, and a lady bass player, Nicki Parrott, and Joe Ascione and Bucky Pizzarelli. And it was for label called Arbors Records.

ctx.x: But I’ve done a lot of film dates. In New York when I was — at sort of the tail end of a certain kind of vintage guitar player, there were guys like Tony Mottola and Bucky Pizzarelli, Barry Galbraith, Howie Collins and Al Caiola, Al Cassamentes. And the younger crew like David Spinozza and — oh the guys are going to hate me for forgetting — I worked a lot with a guy named Jay Berliner, Billy — well anyway, Ralph Casales. We were still getting calls for a lot of recordings and film dates. And I did a lot of stuff…
there was a guy named Donald McDonald for a while. And the guy — oh he’s going to hate me. The guy was from Rochester, he used to play with Chuck—

items.title: Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Gene Bertoncini quit the show and they asked me to do it with Skitch Henderson... Well Doc Severinsen was in the band... I’m sitting there with Al Klink...

ctx.x: Less arranged almost. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Yeah. And then the set groups were playing now. They weren’t using studio guys. Record companies turned over the studios to a group. Now the group would sit around all day long trying to make a track. A rhythm track. And nobody could get in — Mitch Miller couldn’t get into his own studios down there because some group was sitting there trying to make rhythm tracks, and they’re subtracting and adding — take this out, put this in— waste of time. Big waste of time and money. So I didn’t want to get in on that so…
And what was the schedule like for that show?
